title: Ancient Rome · Episode 2
chapters: Hadrian's Wall: life on the edge of an empire

units.t: Ancient Rome. Episode two.
In this episode: Daily life in ancient Rome, Roads, aqueducts and concrete, Hadrian's Wall: life on the edge of an empire and Why Rome fell.
Part one. Daily life in ancient Rome.
Apartment blocks, fast food, public toilets and traffic jams.
Life in Rome was surprisingly familiar.
Crowded city living.
By the time of Augustus, Rome may have held around a million people, probably the largest city in the world, though numbers are debated.
Most lived in insulae, apartment blocks several storeys high, often cheaply built and prone to fire and collapse.
The poorest lived on the top floors, farthest from water and hardest to escape, while shops filled the ground floor.
Augustus capped building height at about 20 metres and set up a firefighting force, the vigiles.
Wealthy families lived in a domus, a private house around an open courtyard.
Traffic was so bad that Julius Caesar banned most wheeled carts from the city in daylight.
Family, slavery, school.
The paterfamilias, the oldest living male, held legal power over his children and grandchildren, including their property, though custom usually softened it.
Women could not vote or hold office, but wealthy women could own property and wield influence.
Slavery was central to the economy, in homes, fields and mines.
Lives could be brutal, yet many urban slaves were freed and could rise, sometimes becoming very rich.
Many babies did not survive infancy.
Children whose parents could pay went from about age seven to a teacher, learning to read, write and count on wax tablets.
Beatings were common.
Richer boys moved on to Greek and Latin literature and rhetoric, the art of persuasion.
Eating and bathing.
Many apartments had no proper kitchen, and cooking upstairs risked fire, so ordinary Romans bought hot food at thermopolia, an ancient fast food.
Pompeii had dozens.
One excavated around 2020 still held traces of duck, pork, goat, fish and snails.
The staple diet was bread, porridge, olive oil, beans and wine mixed with water, flavoured with garum, a fermented fish sauce.
Many Romans visited the baths daily.
A big bathhouse had cold, warm and hot rooms, the hot ones heated by furnaces sending air under raised floors and through walls.
Many also had gardens, snack sellers and libraries, and entry was cheap.
Public latrines had long stone benches with running water beneath.
Bread and circuses.
The Circus Maximus, a huge chariot-racing track, may have held around 150,000 spectators.
Fans passionately followed four racing teams known by their colours: Reds, Whites, Greens and Blues.
Top charioteers became celebrities and earned fortunes.
The Colosseum, opened in AD 80, held about 50,000 people for gladiator fights, animal hunts and public executions.
Gladiators were mostly slaves or prisoners, though some volunteered, and not every fight ended in death.
The state also handed out free or cheap grain to poorer citizens.
The poet Juvenal complained that the people now cared only about 'bread and circuses', a phrase still used for distracting people with food and entertainment instead of real political power.
Gods and Pompeii.
Religion was part of daily routine.
Many homes had a small shrine, the lararium, where families offered food or incense to household spirits.
Public temples honoured Jupiter, Juno and Mars, and Romans readily adopted foreign gods such as Isis.
Saturnalia, held in December, involved feasting, gifts and role reversals in which masters might serve their slaves.
In AD 79, Mount Vesuvius buried Pompeii, near modern Naples, under several metres of ash and pumice.
Excavations have revealed streets, shops and bakeries with carbonised loaves still in the ovens, plus wall paintings and thousands of pieces of graffiti, from election slogans to love notes.
Plaster poured into hollows left by decayed bodies produced casts of victims' final moments.
The key idea: Most Romans lived in cramped, fire-prone apartment blocks in a city of around a million.
Part two. Roads, aqueducts and concrete.
Roman engineers built so well that some of their bridges, roads and domes are still in use two thousand years later.
All roads.
Romans built around 80,000 kilometres of paved roads so armies, officials, traders and messages could move quickly.
They were built in layers of stone, gravel and sand, topped with fitted paving stones and cambered so rain ran off into ditches.
They ran as straight as the landscape allowed, cutting through hills and crossing marshes on embankments.
Milestones marked distances, and relay stations let official messengers change horses.
The Via Appia, begun in 312 BC, survives in long stretches, some with its ancient paving.
Many modern European roads still follow Roman routes, and the saying 'all roads lead to Rome' reflects how the network radiated from the capital.
Water in, waste out.
By the early 200s AD, Rome had eleven aqueducts delivering hundreds of thousands of cubic metres of water a day to fountains, baths and wealthy homes.
They relied on gravity alone, keeping a steady downhill gradient over tens of kilometres, sometimes well under a metre of drop per kilometre.
Most of each channel ran underground.
The arches mainly crossed valleys, as at the Pont du Gard in France.
The Aqua Virgo, finished in 19 BC, still feeds the Trevi Fountain.
Water had to flow out again.
The Cloaca Maxima, traditionally begun in the 500s BC, drained the marshy Forum valley.
Overflow flushed waste into the Tiber, keeping streets cleaner but polluting the river, and many homes were not connected.
Parts of it still carry water today.
The power of arches.
Romans did not invent the arch, but they used it on a massive scale.
An arch is built from wedge-shaped stones, held by a wooden frame until the central keystone goes in, after which it supports itself.
It carries weight around its curve and down into its supports, so it can span wider gaps than a flat stone beam, which would crack.
Line up arches and you get a bridge or aqueduct.
Extend an arch and you get a vault, a curved ceiling.
Rotate it and you get a dome.
Triumphal arches, such as the Arch of Constantine beside the Colosseum, celebrated victories and inspired later monuments like the Arc de Triomphe in Paris.
Concrete and the Pantheon.
Romans mixed lime with volcanic ash called pozzolana, and rubble, to make concrete.
It let them build quickly, in almost any shape, with less skilled labour than carved stone, and some mixes set underwater.
Roman harbour structures have survived 2,000 years of pounding by the sea.
Researchers found that seawater reacted with the ash to grow new minerals that strengthened the concrete.
A 2023 study suggested lime lumps could also help seal cracks.
The Pantheon, rebuilt under Hadrian around AD 125, has a dome about 43 metres across, as high as it is wide.
An open oculus, about 8 metres wide, lets in light.
Lighter volcanic stone near the top and sunken panels reduce weight.
It is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.
Building an empire.
Legionaries carried tools as well as weapons and built a fortified camp each night on campaign.
In 55 BC Caesar's engineers bridged the Rhine in about ten days.
Many European cities began as Roman military bases.
Hadrian's Wall, begun around AD 122, ran about 117 kilometres across northern Britain, and stretches still stand.
Roads moved legions, aqueducts made big cities possible, and grand buildings displayed Rome's wealth.
Surveyors used the groma to lay out straight lines and the chorobates to level.
The architect Vitruvius argued that buildings should be strong, useful and beautiful.
His Ten Books on Architecture inspired Renaissance architects, and its influence shows in the domes, arches and columns of parliaments, banks and museums worldwide, including many in Australia.
The key idea: Roman roads, built in layers and cambered, linked the empire and many still shape European routes.
Part three. Hadrian's Wall: life on the edge of an empire.
For nearly three hundred years, soldiers from across the Roman world guarded a stone wall in the rain of northern Britain.
The letters they left behind are astonishingly human.
The emperor’s frontier.
Hadrian became emperor in AD 117, when the empire was at its largest.
Rather than keep conquering, he consolidated, and around AD 122 he visited Britain.
Construction began soon after.
The wall ran about 118 kilometres, from Wallsend on the Tyne to Bowness-on-Solway, built mainly by the three legions stationed in Britain.
It was more than a line of stone.
The eastern part was stone up to about three metres thick; the western section began as turf and was later rebuilt in stone.
Every Roman mile, about 1.
5 kilometres, stood a small fort called a milecastle with a gateway, and two turrets lay between each pair.
A ditch ran in front, an earthwork called the vallum behind, and around fifteen larger forts, such as Housesteads, were added.
What was it for.
It is tempting to see the wall as a barrier against invading hordes.
Hadrian’s biography, written centuries later, says he built it to separate the Romans from the barbarians.
But most historians think its purpose was more complicated.
Soldiers did not usually fight from the top of walls; they fought in the open, and the many gateways suggest people were expected to pass through, under supervision.
Its main jobs were probably controlling who crossed, collecting customs duties, preventing small-scale raids and cattle rustling, and watching the tribes to the north.
It was also a statement: a massive stone barrier from coast to coast announced the power of Rome.
Historians still debate how much each purpose mattered.
Soldiers from everywhere.
The legionaries who built the wall mostly moved elsewhere once it was finished.
It was garrisoned by auxiliaries, soldiers recruited from the empire’s provinces who became Roman citizens after their service.
Inscriptions show units from what are now Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany, Spain and beyond.
At Arbeia, in modern South Shields, there was even a unit of bargemen from the Tigris river in Mesopotamia.
A tombstone found there was set up by Barates, a man from Palmyra in Syria, for his wife Regina, a freed slave from the British Catuvellauni tribe.
It carries an inscription in Latin and a line in Palmyrene Aramaic.
The northern frontier was one of the most multicultural places in Roman Britain.
Postcards from Vindolanda.
Just south of the wall lies Vindolanda, a fort that predates Hadrian’s Wall.
From 1973, archaeologists there led by Robin Birley began finding thin wooden tablets, preserved in waterlogged, oxygen-free soil, covered in ink handwriting from around AD 100.
They include duty reports, supply lists and private letters.
One soldier is sent socks, sandals and two pairs of underpants.
Another note dismissively calls the locals Brittunculi, little Britons.
The most famous is a birthday invitation from Claudia Severa to her friend Sulpicia Lepidina, the wife of the fort’s commander.
A scribe wrote most of it, but a few warm lines at the end appear to be in Claudia’s own hand, among the earliest known examples of Latin handwriting by a woman.
The wall today.
A common myth is that Hadrian’s Wall marks the border between England and Scotland.
It does not.
The whole wall lies within England, and in places the modern border is up to about a hundred kilometres to the north.

Around AD 142, Hadrian’s successor Antoninus Pius pushed further into what is now Scotland and built the turf Antonine Wall, but it was abandoned within about twenty years and the army returned to Hadrian’s line.
The wall was garrisoned until Roman rule in Britain ended in the early fifth century.
Afterwards, much of its stone was taken to build farms, churches and roads.
Even so, long stretches still stand, and since 1987 it has been listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The key idea: Hadrian chose to consolidate the empire, and his soldiers built a fortified wall of milecastles, forts and ditches across northern Britain.
Part four. Why Rome fell.
Historians have offered hundreds of reasons for the fall of Rome.
The truth is a slow, complicated unravelling, and half the empire didn't fall at all.
Crisis and division.
The first two centuries of the empire, the Pax Romana, brought relative stability and trade from Britain to Syria.
Then, from AD 235 to 284, Rome had over 20 emperors, most murdered or killed in battle.
Invasions, civil wars, plague and runaway inflation, as emperors debased silver coins to pay soldiers, battered the empire.
In 260 the Persians captured Emperor Valerian.
Aurelian reunited the empire by 274.
Diocletian decided the empire was too big for one ruler and shared power among four emperors in 293.
Constantine emerged from the civil war that followed and founded Constantinople in 330.
After Theodosius died in 395, the empire was permanently divided into a Western Empire and a richer, more populous Eastern Empire.
Money and borders.
The late empire needed a larger army, probably several hundred thousand soldiers, and paying it was a constant struggle.
Diocletian's price controls in 301 largely failed.
Taxes rose, and laws tied farmers to their land so taxes could be collected.
Rome relied more on Germanic recruits and allied groups, called foederati, whose loyalty was never guaranteed.
In the late 300s the Huns pushed Germanic peoples such as the Goths west.
Allowed across the Danube in 376, the Goths were mistreated and rebelled, crushing a Roman army at Adrianople in 378.
Visigoths, Vandals, Burgundians and Franks settled inside the empire.
In 410 Alaric's Visigoths sacked Rome, the first time in about 800 years.
The last emperor.
The Vandals captured Carthage in 439, seizing some of the West's richest provinces and their grain and taxes.
Attila, who led the Huns from 434 until 453, extracted huge payments of gold from the East.
In 451 he invaded Gaul and was stopped at the Catalaunian Plains by a Roman and Visigothic army.
He turned back from Italy the next year, though famine and disease probably mattered more than Pope Leo I.
In 455 the Vandals sacked Rome.
Western emperors were by then puppets of powerful generals.
In 476 Odoacer deposed the teenage Romulus Augustulus and ruled Italy as king.
Life did not change overnight: new kingdoms often kept Roman laws, Latin, towns and the church.
No single cause.
The historian Alexander Demandt collected more than 200 proposed causes, from lead poisoning to moral decay.
Edward Gibbon partly blamed Christianity, a view most historians now see as too simple.
Most point to a mix.
Constant civil wars wasted soldiers and money.
Taxes rose, and the loss of rich provinces cut revenue.
Plagues, and possibly climate shifts, played roles.
Meanwhile, migrating peoples found an empire less able to resist.
Some historians prefer to speak of a 'transformation' as Roman and Germanic cultures blended.
Others stress a real collapse in living standards.
The empire that survived.
The Eastern half, called the Byzantine Empire by historians, was ruled from Constantinople.
Its people mostly spoke Greek but called themselves Romans.

Under Justinian in the 500s it reconquered North Africa, Italy and part of Spain, built Hagia Sophia and produced a law code, later called the Corpus Juris Civilis, that shaped legal systems across Europe.
Byzantine scholars preserved many ancient Greek texts, and scholars who moved west helped feed the Renaissance.
Constantinople finally fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1453, an event often treated as the true end of the Roman Empire.
The key idea: After two peaceful centuries, a chaotic crisis in the AD 200s led to the empire being split in two.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why were Roman apartment blocks dangerous for the poor?
Answer. They were cheaply built and prone to fire.
Question two. Why were Roman roads built in layers and cambered?
Answer. So they drained well and lasted.
Question three. What is Hadrian’s Wall best described as?
Answer. A wall with milecastles, turrets, ditches and forts.
Question four. Why did Diocletian share power among four emperors?
Answer. He judged the empire too big for one ruler.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
